subtopics.name: Increased intracranial pressure and head injury

questions.stem: A client had a total parathyroidectomy 18 hours ago. The client reports numbness around the mouth and in the fingertips and muscle cramps in the hands. When the nurse taps in front of the ear, the corner of the mouth twitches. Serum calcium is 6.8 mg/dL, and the ECG shows a prolonged QT interval. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Notify the provider and prepare IV calcium gluconate as prescribed
Keep emergency airway equipment at the bedside
Give a potassium supplement for the muscle cramps
Encourage the client to breathe into a paper bag
Restrict dairy foods until the calcium returns to normal

parameters.text: Color and clarity of the urine
Bowel sounds in each of the four quadrants
Body weight measured once a week

rationale.correct: After parathyroid or thyroid surgery, watch for hypocalcemia: tingling, cramps, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, laryngospasm and long QT; treat with IV calcium.

perOption.c1: Perioral numbness, cramps, a positive Chvostek sign, low calcium and a long QT after parathyroid surgery show acute hypocalcemia.
perOption.c2: Hyperkalemia causes peaked T waves, not these neuromuscular signs.
perOption.c3: Thyroid storm causes fever and tachycardia.
perOption.c4: Hyperventilation can cause tingling, but the low calcium and Chvostek sign point to hypocalcemia.
perOption.a2: Laryngospasm can occur with severe hypocalcemia.
perOption.a4: The symptoms are from low calcium, not hyperventilation.
perOption.a5: Calcium intake is needed, not restricted.
perOption.p2: Airway and rhythm problems are the dangerous complications.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is monitoring several clients on telemetry. For each rhythm and situation, indicate the first action the nurse should expect.

rows.text: Sinus tachycardia at 124/min in a client with a fever of 39 °C (102.2 °F)
Ventricular fibrillation in a client who is unresponsive with no pulse
Asystole confirmed in two leads in a client with no pulse
Narrow-complex regular tachycardia at 192/min in a stable, alert client

rationale.correct: Treat sinus tachycardia's cause; defibrillate VF or pulseless VT; give CPR and epinephrine for asystole and PEA; try vagal maneuvers then adenosine for stable SVT.

perOption.r1:c1: Sinus tachycardia is treated by finding and treating the cause, such as fever.
perOption.r1:c4: Vagal maneuvers are not used for sinus tachycardia.
perOption.r2:c1: Not the first action in cardiac arrest.
perOption.r2:c2: VF is treated with immediate defibrillation.
perOption.r2:c3: CPR continues, but defibrillation is the key first step.
perOption.r3:c3: CPR and epinephrine are the treatment for asystole.
perOption.r4:c4: Stable SVT is first treated with vagal maneuvers, then adenosine.

references: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care

questions.stem: On the first morning after a hip replacement, the nurse reviews the client's laboratory results. Highlight the results that need prompt reporting.

rationale.correct: After surgery, report significant drops in hemoglobin, rising creatinine and significant electrolyte abnormalities; mild stress hyperglycemia is common.

perOption.r1: A large drop suggests significant blood loss.
perOption.r3: A doubling of creatinine suggests acute kidney injury.
perOption.r4: Mild stress hyperglycemia after surgery is common.
perOption.r5: Significant hyponatremia can cause confusion and seizures.

questions.stem: The nurse is inserting a nasogastric tube for decompression. Place the steps in order.

items.text: Confirm placement as policy directs, such as pH testing of aspirate and x-ray
Raise the head of the bed to high Fowler's and have the client flex the neck slightly
Insert the tube while the client sips water or swallows, advancing to the mark
Measure the tube from the tip of the nose to the earlobe to the xiphoid process and mark it

rationale.correct: NG insertion: measure, position upright with the neck flexed, advance with swallowing and confirm placement.

perOption.a: Estimates the length to reach the stomach.
perOption.b: Positioning eases passage into the esophagus.
perOption.c: Swallowing helps direct the tube into the esophagus.

questions.stem: A client is scheduled for a bronchoscopy with moderate sedation this morning. Which actions should the nurse take before the procedure? Select all that apply.

options.text: Confirm the client has been NPO for the required time
Check that informed consent is signed
Ask about anticoagulant use and bleeding problems
Give the client a large breakfast to keep up their strength
Remove dentures and check the airway
Tell the client they will be awake and can talk throughout

rationale.correct: Before bronchoscopy: NPO, consent, anticoagulant review, remove dentures and prepare for sedation monitoring.

perOption.e: Prepares for the scope and sedation.
perOption.f: The client is sedated and cannot speak with the scope in place.

questions.stem: A client has just had a percutaneous liver biopsy. How should the nurse position the client?

options.text: Left side-lying with the head of the bed raised
Right side-lying with a pillow under the ribs
Prone with the arms above the head
High Fowler's with the legs dangling

rationale.correct: After liver biopsy, place the client on the right side for several hours to compress the site and watch for bleeding.

perOption.a: Left side-lying does not compress the biopsy site.
perOption.b: Lying on the right side presses on the puncture site and helps prevent bleeding.
perOption.c: Prone is not the standard position after liver biopsy.
perOption.d: Upright positioning does not compress the liver.

questions.stem: Before drawing an arterial blood gas from a client's radial artery, the nurse performs a modified Allen test. The hand stays pale for 12 seconds after the ulnar artery is released. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Draw the sample from the radial artery as planned
Do not use that radial artery; choose another site
Apply a warm compress for 10 minutes and then draw from the same artery
Repeat the test on the same hand until the color returns faster

rationale.correct: A positive modified Allen test (color returns after more than about 5 to 10 seconds) means poor ulnar flow; avoid that radial artery.

perOption.a: Poor ulnar flow means the hand may lose blood supply if the radial artery is damaged.
perOption.b: A delayed return of color shows poor collateral flow; another site should be used.
perOption.c: Warming does not fix inadequate collateral circulation.
perOption.d: Repeating does not change the anatomy.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A 70-year-old client with watery diarrhea for 5 days and dry mucous membranes has arterial blood gases: pH 7.32, PaCO2 30 mm Hg, HCO3 15 mEq/L. Complete the sentence.

content.template: These results show {{b1}} that is {{b2}}, most likely caused by {{b3}}.

options.text: metabolic acidosis
respiratory acidosis
metabolic alkalosis
partly compensated
fully compensated
uncompensated
loss of bicarbonate in the stool
vomiting stomach acid
hypoventilation

rationale.correct: Diarrhea causes bicarbonate loss and metabolic acidosis; the lungs compensate by blowing off CO2.

perOption.b1:a: Low pH with low bicarbonate is metabolic acidosis.
perOption.b2:a: PaCO2 has fallen as the lungs compensate, but pH is still low.
perOption.b2:c: The low PaCO2 shows the lungs are compensating.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A 78-year-old client with type 2 diabetes is brought in after a week of poor intake and increasing confusion. Blood glucose is 912 mg/dL, serum osmolality 362 mOsm/kg, sodium 152 mEq/L (corrected higher), pH 7.36, bicarbonate 23 mEq/L and urine ketones are trace. Blood pressure is 92/54 mm Hg and heart rate 118/min. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Give large volumes of IV isotonic fluid as prescribed
Start an insulin infusion after fluids are under way, as prescribed
Give a bolus of subcutaneous long-acting insulin and fluids later
Restrict fluids to prevent cerebral edema
Give sodium bicarbonate to correct the pH

parameters.text: Bowel sounds in each of the four quadrants
Body weight measured once a week
Pupil size and reaction to light

rationale.correct: HHS: severe dehydration and hyperosmolality without major ketoacidosis; give fluids first, then insulin, and correct glucose and osmolality gradually.

perOption.c1: Very high glucose and osmolality, severe dehydration and confusion without significant acidosis or ketones is HHS.
perOption.c2: pH and bicarbonate are near normal and ketones are minimal.
perOption.c3: Confusion here is explained by hyperosmolality.
perOption.a1: Severe dehydration is the main problem; fluids come first.
perOption.a2: Insulin is given after fluid replacement has started.
perOption.a3: IV fluids come first, and insulin is given by infusion.
perOption.p1: Gradual correction lowers the risk of cerebral edema.
perOption.p2: Show response to fluids and treatment.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
American Diabetes Association Standards of Care

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize and manage HHS.

questions.stem: For each set of findings, indicate the type of shock it most likely represents.

rows.text: Cool, pale skin, low CVP, tachycardia and a recent GI bleed
Crackles, distended neck veins and low blood pressure after a large MI
Fever, warm flushed skin, wide pulse pressure and low blood pressure
Hypotension, heart rate 48/min and warm dry skin after a cervical spine injury

rationale.correct: Shock types: hypovolemic (cool, tachycardic, low CVP), cardiogenic (congestion), early septic (warm, wide pulse pressure) and neurogenic (warm, bradycardic).

perOption.r1:c1: Blood loss with low filling pressures is hypovolemic shock.
perOption.r1:c2: Cardiogenic shock has high filling pressures.
perOption.r2:c2: Pump failure with congestion is cardiogenic shock.
perOption.r3:c3: Early septic shock causes vasodilation with warm skin.
perOption.r4:c4: Loss of sympathetic tone causes neurogenic shock.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Distinguish types of shock.

questions.stem: A client with severe COPD and a history of CO2 retention is admitted with an exacerbation. SpO2 is 84% on room air, and the client is alert. Which oxygen plan should the nurse expect?

options.text: High-flow oxygen by non-rebreather mask to bring the SpO2 to 100%
Controlled oxygen to an SpO2 of 88% to 92%
No oxygen, because oxygen stops the client's drive to breathe
Oxygen at night, while the client is asleep

rationale.correct: In COPD with CO2 retention, titrate oxygen to an SpO2 of 88% to 92%, watch for rising CO2 and drowsiness and never withhold oxygen for hypoxemia.

perOption.a: Too much oxygen in CO2 retainers can worsen hypercapnia.
perOption.b: A target of 88% to 92% corrects hypoxemia while limiting CO2 retention.
perOption.c: Hypoxemia must be treated; oxygen is titrated, not withheld.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client has full-thickness circumferential burns of the chest from a house fire. Over 2 hours, breathing becomes shallow and the ventilator pressures rise, although the airway is clear on suctioning. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Increasing the sedation so the client fights the ventilator less
An escharotomy to release the tight chest eschar
Giving a diuretic to reduce fluid in the lungs
Changing the endotracheal tube to a larger size

rationale.correct: Circumferential full-thickness burns of the chest or limbs can restrict breathing or blood flow; escharotomy is needed.

perOption.a: The problem is the stiff burned skin restricting chest movement, not agitation.
perOption.b: Circumferential chest eschar restricts expansion; escharotomy restores ventilation.
perOption.c: The chest wall restriction is the cause.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the need for escharotomy.

questions.stem: A stable, alert client in supraventricular tachycardia at 196/min did not convert with vagal maneuvers. The provider prescribes adenosine 6 mg IV. How should the nurse give it?

options.text: Dilute it in 100 mL of saline and infuse it over 30 minutes by pump
Push it rapidly in a proximal vein, then flush fast with saline
Push it slowly over 5 minutes while watching the monitor closely
Give it intramuscularly into the deltoid

rationale.correct: Adenosine: rapid IV push in a proximal vein followed by a rapid saline flush; warn the client about a brief feeling of chest pressure and expect a short pause.

perOption.a: Adenosine has a half-life of seconds and must be given as a rapid push.
perOption.b: A rapid push and flush gets the drug to the heart before it breaks down; a brief pause in rhythm is expected.
perOption.c: A slow push lets the drug break down before reaching the heart.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care

questions.stem: Review the 1500 findings. Highlight the findings that require immediate follow-up.

segments.text: sharp chest pain on breathing in and a cough
Pain rated 9 of 10 in the back and legs
a new infiltrate in the right lower lobe

rationale.correct: In sickle cell crisis, new chest pain, hypoxemia and a new infiltrate signal acute chest syndrome, a leading cause of death.

perOption.s2: Chest symptoms in sickle cell disease may be acute chest syndrome.
perOption.s4: Expected in a vaso-occlusive crisis and needs treatment, but chest findings are more dangerous.
perOption.s6: Falling oxygen saturation suggests acute chest syndrome.
perOption.s8: A new infiltrate with chest symptoms defines acute chest syndrome.
perOption.s10: A falling hemoglobin may need transfusion.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize acute chest syndrome.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence based on the client's data.

content.template: The client is having a vaso-occlusive crisis complicated by {{b1}}, likely triggered by {{b2}}.

options.text: acute chest syndrome
an asthma attack
a heart attack
dehydration and low oxygen during a long flight
eating a high-iron meal
too much exercise

rationale.correct: Dehydration, hypoxia, cold, infection and stress trigger sickling; acute chest syndrome is a serious complication.

perOption.b1:a: Chest pain, fever, hypoxemia and a new infiltrate define acute chest syndrome.
perOption.b1:b: There is no wheezing, and the infiltrate points to acute chest syndrome.
perOption.b1:c: The picture fits acute chest syndrome.
perOption.b2:b: Diet is not a trigger here.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.educationalObjective: Analyze triggers and complications of sickle cell crisis.

questions.stem: For each complication, indicate whether the client is at high or low immediate risk based on the current data.

rows.text: Respiratory failure
Worsening anemia needing transfusion
Sepsis
Hyperglycemia

rationale.correct: Acute chest syndrome threatens breathing; anemia and infection risk are high because of hemolysis and loss of spleen function.

perOption.r1:c1: Falling SpO2 and rising respiratory rate with an infiltrate show high risk.
perOption.r3:c1: Fever and a high WBC in a client with functional asplenia show high risk.
perOption.r4:c1: Nothing in the data suggests high glucose.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize complications in sickle cell crisis.

questions.stem: Which interventions should the nurse anticipate for this client? Select all that apply.

options.text: Oxygen to keep the SpO2 at or above 95% or per protocol
IV fluids for hydration
Incentive spirometry every 1 to 2 hours while awake
Blood cultures and broad-spectrum antibiotics
Cold packs on the painful legs
Strict bed rest without changing position

rationale.correct: Acute chest syndrome care: oxygen, hydration, incentive spirometry, antibiotics, pain control and possible transfusion; avoid cold.

perOption.b: Hydration reduces sickling, with care to avoid overload.
perOption.c: Prevents atelectasis that worsens acute chest syndrome.
perOption.d: Fever and an infiltrate need antibiotics.
perOption.e: Cold causes vasoconstriction and worsens sickling.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.educationalObjective: Plan care for acute chest syndrome.

questions.stem: The client still rates pain 9 of 10 one hour after arrival. Which pain management approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Give oral acetaminophen and wait an hour to see whether it is enough
Give IV opioids promptly, then scheduled or by PCA
Give meperidine at 3-hour intervals as the preferred opioid
Withhold opioids because the client might be seeking drugs

rationale.correct: Treat sickle cell crisis pain quickly with IV opioids (scheduled or PCA), reassess often and avoid meperidine.

perOption.a: Severe crisis pain needs strong analgesia.
perOption.b: Sickle cell crisis pain needs rapid, scheduled IV opioids with close monitoring.
perOption.c: Meperidine can cause seizures and is avoided.
perOption.d: Assuming drug seeking leads to undertreated pain.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: Compare the 2200 and 0200 data. Highlight the findings that require immediate action.

rationale.correct: A falling GCS, a dilating pupil and Cushing's triad (widening pulse pressure, bradycardia, irregular breathing) signal rising ICP and possible herniation.

perOption.r1: A drop of 6 points shows serious neurological decline.
perOption.r2: A dilating, sluggish pupil on the side of injury suggests herniation.
perOption.r3: Widening pulse pressure is part of Cushing's triad.
perOption.r4: Mild temperature rise; manage, but it is not the most urgent.
perOption.r5: Irregular breathing is part of Cushing's triad.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cues of rising intracranial pressure.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence based on the client's data.

content.template: The client's findings show {{b1}}, and the right-sided pupil change suggests {{b2}}.

options.text: rising intracranial pressure
a seizure
hypoglycemia
pressure on the right third cranial nerve from herniation
a normal effect of opioid pain medication
an eye injury from the fall

rationale.correct: Rising ICP shows as a falling level of consciousness, pupil changes and Cushing's triad; a dilating pupil on one side suggests herniation.

perOption.b1:a: A falling GCS and Cushing's triad show rising ICP.
perOption.b2:a: A dilating pupil on the side of injury suggests uncal herniation.
perOption.b2:c: The neurological pattern points to herniation.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.educationalObjective: Analyze cues of brain herniation.

questions.stem: Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

condition.text: Rising intracranial pressure with impending herniation

actions.text: Notify the provider now and prepare for treatment
Raise the head of the bed to 30 degrees, head midline
Lay the client flat to improve blood flow to the brain
Cluster all care together to finish quickly
Suction the airway every 30 minutes routinely

parameters.text: Glasgow Coma Scale and pupil checks
Blood pressure, heart rate and breathing pattern
Bowel sounds in each of the four quadrants
Color and clarity of the urine

rationale.correct: Impending herniation: notify immediately, raise the head of the bed to 30 degrees with the head midline and expect hyperosmolar therapy; monitor GCS, pupils and vital signs.

perOption.c1: Falling GCS, a dilating pupil and Cushing's triad point to herniation.
perOption.c3: Opioids cause pinpoint pupils, not a dilated one.
perOption.c4: Blood pressure is high, not low.
perOption.a2: Improves venous drainage and lowers ICP.
perOption.a4: Clustering many activities can raise ICP; spacing care is better.
perOption.a5: Suctioning raises ICP and is done only when needed.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize care for rising intracranial pressure.

questions.stem: Which measures help lower intracranial pressure for this client? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the head and neck in a neutral, midline position
Keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees
Maintain normal oxygen and carbon dioxide levels
Keep the room quiet and space out care activities
Encourage the client to cough forcefully every hour
Bend the hips sharply with pillows under the knees
Treat fever promptly as prescribed

rationale.correct: Lower ICP by keeping the head midline and raised 30 degrees, maintaining normal gases, reducing stimulation and avoiding coughing, straining and hip flexion.

perOption.a: Prevents compression of the jugular veins.
perOption.c: Low oxygen or high CO2 raises ICP.
perOption.f: Hip flexion raises intra-abdominal and intracranial pressure.
perOption.g: Fever raises metabolic demand and ICP.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Use measures to lower intracranial pressure.

questions.stem: The provider prescribes IV mannitol for the rising ICP. Which assessment is most important while the client receives this drug?

options.text: Checking the blood glucose on the hour
Urine output, osmolality and electrolytes
Measuring the abdominal girth at the umbilicus each shift
Checking the client's hearing in both ears once each shift

rationale.correct: Mannitol pulls water from the brain and causes diuresis; monitor urine output, osmolality, electrolytes and signs of fluid imbalance.

perOption.a: Glucose is not the main concern with mannitol.
perOption.b: Mannitol causes osmotic diuresis; urine output, osmolality and electrolytes guide safe use.
perOption.d: Hearing is not the main concern.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

Clear fluid draining from the nose that tests positive for glucose

caseStudies.title: Rising intracranial pressure after a head injury

exhibits.title: Neurosurgical ICU, 0200
exhibits.body: A 34-year-old client was admitted 10 hours ago after a fall from a ladder with a right frontal contusion. At 2200 the client was drowsy but opened eyes to voice, obeyed commands and was oriented. At 0200 the client opens eyes only to pain, makes incomprehensible sounds and withdraws from pain. The right pupil is 6 mm and sluggish; the left is 3 mm and brisk.
